Today it's a trivial job to generate random bingo cards with a computer and print them out. But before computers were commonplace, how did printing presses create bingo cards, and do it quickly? It seems like an interesting mechanical puzzle to me. A google search didn't turn up any information.

Does anybody know how it was done? Any pictures of a mechanized printing press generating random cards?

Edit: Bingo cards dammit. Looking forward to some funny answers.
How were randomized bingo cars printed before the age of computers?

From the Wikipedia entry on bingo cards, relevant text below: Link

Before the advent of printing machines, numbers on bingo cards were either painted by hand or stamped using rubber stamps onto thick cardboard.

The cards were also reusable, so they would use a token instead of a marker drawn on to the card so the card could be used again, important in a time where the paper would have been more expensive.

Further to this, I can recall seeing bingo cards in my youth that were made of thick cardboard had had built in translucent slides over the numbers instead of tokens. So the cards were completely reusable and didn't have the annoyance of dropping your bingo tokens everywhere.

Unfortunately it doesn't say anything about how it was done -after- the advent of the printing press. Bingo has been played with single-use disposable cards for at least 40 years (just going back to my own memories of church bingo games that my mother organized). They used cards similar to this:

http://www.wholesalebingosupplies.com/bingo-paper/bingo-paper-sheets/3-vertical-bingo-paper.html

And they used -a lot- of them. Easily a few thousand for each night's bingo.

I'm wondering how a print shop in 1975 managed to print thousands and thousands of bingo cards with random (but following the rules of bingo) number patterns on them. Did they pluck metal dies randomly from a set and position them over the paper? Were cards printed one number at a time or all at once? Were the dies attached to wheels? How did they avoid putting two copies of the number '5' in the B column (just as an example)?

I think it's highly unlikely that a printing company in 1975 could do this with computers, and I'm guessing that single-use paper cards were in use long before that.

Well if they want a uniform distribution, print one of each combination and shuffle them.

But if that was too many combinations, I'm sure it wouldn't be hard to spin a wheel of some sort before each card is made, which would be akin to rolling a dice.

But that being said - are we really sure their bingo cards were really random? It would be easy to get away with without computers.

So, it seems like the question you have is how the bingo numbers were randomized before good psuedorand functions were available.

And to answer that, you have to realize that for random results you only need one of the inputs to the system to be random, not all.

So for the bingo cards, they would have a fair number of different card faces available -- essentially just enough to make the odds of two people in the same hall having the same cardface be zero -- and then rely on the ball call for the random element.

So it doesn't really matter too much that the numbers on the card was 1) pulled out of some humans ass and 2) not really that random, since the other input to the system, the order of numbers that are pulled from the hopper, is for all intents and purposes random.

TL;DR: 1d75 compared to [set 1|set 2|set3|...] is exactly as random as 1d75.
